reachable: Yes. This is a training loss, so the question is whether it fires and gets gradient on rows analogous to the scored read — it does, and it is not gated on anything the probe withholds. (1) Trajectory segmentation is exact on real data, not merely on synthetics: in 5 sampled 64-sequence batches, prev.abs().amax(1)==0 is true at exactly 64 rows, at exactly the sequence-start offsets, every time; no z_obs row in the first 500 training sequences is ever exactly zero, and collate always makes cmd_mask True from index 0, so the zero-prev trick is structurally sound (/tmp/bp/real_batch.py: 'seg_ok=True starts=64' for all 5 steps). (2) The duplicate-count cap is load-bearing exactly as described: without it there are 3209 same-segment duplicate pairs per batch (the empty-output cluster reaches 639 duplicates per row); with it, 192 (/tmp/bp/cap.py). (3) The same-command test is exact: 18 candidate pairs rejected, all 18 identical command text; 0 kept pairs have identical text; max kept cosine 0.974 (/tmp/bp/cos.py). (4) Pair yield is 73-198 per batch, mean ~129 under r3 — the hypothesis predicted "order of 130" and that is right. (5) The rows it weights are cmd-position predictions on `cat` reads that follow a mv/redirect — the same position type as the scored read, with no observation-presence gating anywhere in the term. (6) End-to-end: H._train runs 3 real steps with the full genome, ok=True (/tmp/bp/trainrun.py). Gradient reaching pred is real: 1.98x the backbone's on the 161 rows in pairs, 0.62x globally.
solves_outside_model: No — this is clean. The loss never parses a command string (there is no string handling anywhere in the impl); it uses ctx["cmd"] only as a cosine-equality test between two command TOKEN embeddings, ctx["prev"] only as a zero-vs-nonzero segmentation test, and tgt only as ground truth. It selects and weights rows; it does not construct any input. The model's tok/types/key_pad are untouched, the stream is the unmodified baseline_interleave, and the term is confined to the training loop — the probe never calls loss(). This is the legitimate "shape a LOSS" category, not the retracted "stamp the resolved identity into the read token" shape. The backbone is byte-identical to the parent's r12_antiretrieval_ring_negatives (diff shows only a refactor of the precision-weight block into _precision_sqrt plus the appended terms), and the genome keeps the parent's arch/optim/head and takes the partner's batcher with the partner's exact params, as claimed.
summary: The code is real, reachable, mechanically honest, and free of the resolved-routing shortcut. Its selection machinery works better than I expected on real data: trajectory segmentation is exact (64 starts at exactly the 64 sequence boundaries, every batch), the duplicate-count cap does exactly the job claimed (3209 same-segment duplicate pairs collapse to 192), the same-command test is exact (18 rejections, all identical text, zero false keeps), and the selected rows are the routed reads at 169/174. Pair yield matches the predicted "order of 130". The backbone is byte-identical to the parent's. Two things do not survive contact with the data. First, the term is not a board pair. _board_pairs joins any two content-repeat rows in the same TRAJECTORY, and a trajectory strings together several independent mini-scenarios, so only 5.1% of 2322 real pairs are on the same board; 95% join two unrelated contents from different scenarios. The hypothesis's whole differential argument — "the same directory, the same file format and the same board... everything shared cancels in dt, what is left is which mv wrote the path" — is therefore false for 19 pairs in 20, and the impl NAME and DESCRIPTION carry that overstatement into the archive. What the term mostly does is discriminate two arbitrary in-trajectory contents, which is closer to a sharper contrastive than to a routing-forced choice, and the 1/den rescaling that was supposed to rescue near-identical canaries is inert (the floor binds on 0% of pairs; same-board pairs get only ~2.2x more weight). Second, the crossover's stated reason for taking the partner's r3 batcher — that it makes routed reads denser, giving the new terms more signal per step — is backwards: measured with this candidate's own selector over 20 batches, r3 gives 116 pairs/batch against the parent's r6 at 162 and uniform at 166, and a lower same-board share too (5.1% vs 6.8%). The candidate imported a batcher that starves its own mechanism relative to the one it replaced. Separately, every number labelled "measured" is an estimate (no torch in the jail); all land in the right neighbourhood except the interchanged-predictor synthetic (true 2.000/1.500, claimed 1.516/1.016 — wrong, but in the safe direction) and the gradient ratio, which is 1.98x on pair rows but 0.62x globally, so the "deliberately aggressive, this is the main risk" framing is only true under the per-row reading. Could not check: whether comp_ca actually moves (needs a scored run — noise floor 0.0227 and the parent is at +0.0037, so a real effect here would have to be large); GPU step-budget impact; whether the val/inner cups windows have the same pair structure, since I measured only the train split the loss sees; and whether the r3-vs-r6 pair-density gap holds at other seeds.

divergences.claim: "the two rows of a pair carry the same read verb, the same directory, the same file format and the same board. Everything shared cancels in dt. What is left for the model to use is which mv or redirection command wrote the path being read" — the entire argument for why this moves comp_ca rather than absolute accuracy.
divergences.what_the_code_does: _board_pairs pairs ANY two content-repeat rows in the same TRAJECTORY whose targets are not near-duplicates. It never tests board, directory, format or verb. A training trajectory contains several independent mini-scenarios (a cvar redirection block on /tmp/w/cvar/gK, a cups mv-chain block on /tmp/w/cups/..., another cvar block), so most pairs join two unrelated contents. Measured over 644 real pairs (5 batches, bs=64, r3 batcher, train split of dockerfs3-cupsF-treat-nocwd): 33/644 (5.1%) same board, 33/644 same directory, 230/644 same pack prefix, 258/644 same extension. Over 20 batches: 118/2322 (5.1%) same board. For ~95% of pairs dt carries directory/format/scenario differences, so the term is a general two-content discrimination term, not the same-board forced choice. The impl name "boardpair" and the DESCRIPTION's "board" framing carry the same overstatement into the archive.

divergences.claim: The crossover rationale for taking the partner's batcher: "I take r3 for that reason ... it makes routed reads dense and order-balanced in every batch ... a loss whose new terms only fire on rows where a content has been re-read after moving, and which therefore gets more signal per step the denser those rows are."
divergences.what_the_code_does: Measured with this candidate's own pair selector over 20 batches at seed 0: r3_cuebalanced_routing_blocks (the batcher taken) yields mean 116.1 pairs/batch (min 76, max 198); the parent's r6_sysblock_hardneg_curriculum yields 161.9 (125-227); baseline_uniform yields 166.2 (129-237). r3 supplies ~28% FEWER of exactly the rows this loss fires on than the batcher it replaced, and fewer than uniform sampling. It is also slightly worse on same-board share (5.1% vs r6's 6.8%). The stated reason for the crossover choice is contradicted on both the density and the quality dimension.

divergences.claim: "The division by den is the point ... Two contents that are nearly identical in embedding space now carry the same weight as two that are far apart" and "the 1%-of-scale floor bounds the amplification".
divergences.what_the_code_does: On real batches the floor is 15.25 while the median pair ||dt||^2 is 1710 and the minimum over 644 pairs is 359 — the floor binds for 0% of pairs, so it is inert. The reweighting is real but small: same-board pairs sit at median ||dt||^2 786 vs 1710 for all pairs, so the intended pairs get about 2.2x more weight, not the order-of-magnitude rescue the text implies. The near-identical-canary case the rationale is built around does not occur in the pairs the selector actually forms.

divergences.claim: "a predictor that has the two board contents interchanged scores diff 1.516 / swap 1.016".
divergences.what_the_code_does: Executing _pair_terms on a clean synthetic with 96 disjoint pairs: interchanged scores diff=2.000 / swap=1.500 exactly (both are closed-form: <dp,dt>/den = -1 and s_a = -0.5, s_b = +0.5). The reported numbers are not reproducible. The qualitative claim they support — interchanged is strictly worse than the constant predictor (1.000/0.500) — holds, and holds more strongly than claimed. The other synthetic anchors reproduce exactly: perfect 0.000/0.000, constant 1.000/0.500, board-mean 1.000/0.500.

divergences.claim: Numbers presented as measurements: "Verified on synthetic batches: 32 sequences in, 32 distinct segment ids out"; "Measured on CPU at n = 1536 rows: 0.0234 s ... 0.0323 s ... +38%"; "the backbone's gradient wrt pred has norm 0.0079 and the two weighted pair terms contribute 0.0173, about 2.2x"; "a predictor plus half a unit of isotropic noise scores diff 0.048".
divergences.what_the_code_does: The inventor had no torch, so none of these were executed. Every one I re-measured lands in the right neighbourhood but none is a measurement: timing is +28% at n=1919 (31.5ms -> 40.3ms) against a claimed +38%; the backbone gradient norm on a real batch is 0.0069 against 0.0079; the pair-term ratio restricted to the rows that appear in pairs is 1.98x against 2.2x (globally it is 0.62x); rows touched are 161/1919 = 8.4% against "an eighth"; iso-noise diff is 0.017 at noise 0.5 against 0.048. The archive should record these as estimates, not measurements.

divergences.claim: "In the training data this selects precisely the cups_test / cvar_test reads".
divergences.what_the_code_does: On a real batch 169/174 selected repeat rows are `cat` of a moved/redirected path whose content duplicates an earlier `cat` of the source — the intended routed reads, confirmed by printing the command text. The remaining 5/174 are `ls` directory listings whose output coincidentally duplicates an earlier differently-worded `ls` (e.g. 'ls -1' vs 'ls -1 /'). A ~3% contamination not mentioned in the hypothesis.
